mu_name_from: MuMain ZzzOpenData.cpp maps MODEL_SWORD + i to Sword{i+1}, so Sword02.bmd is sword index 1, which openmu names the Short Sword. MuWeapons.cs agrees from the client's side: `new("Short Sword", "Sword02.bmd", WeaponStance.Sword, ...)`.
why_this_one:
It is the sword a Budge Dragon can afford, and until it existed the pool had no sword in it at all. The Budge Dragon is level 4 - mu.db's monster_kinds row 2 - and the drop pool is level-gated by Loot.Affordable with no per-monster table, so what it leaves is every row at drop level 4 or under. The Kris already built is drop level 6 and out of reach; this is drop level 3 and in it.

That gap was the whole of the sword group's absence from the low pool: the first sword you find in MU is not the first sword in the table.

stats.note: The item's own row, which is what decides the damage, the swing rate and who is allowed to hold it. Copied from OpenMU's 0.75 initialiser rather than restated, so the call it came from is written out beside it and the two can be read against each other in one glance.
stats.from: openmu/src/Persistence/Initialization/Version075/Items/Weapons.cs line 90. The 0.75 table, which is the version this server is being built to.
stats.drop_level_note: The lowest monster that may leave this, and whether one ever does. Three is the number that puts it in a Budge Dragon's pool and keeps it out of a Spider's: the Spider is level 2, so it can afford the Small Axe at 1 and the Apple at 1 and not this. See shared/Loot.cs, where the gate is the rule and not a table.
stats.width_note: width is carried because it is where OpenMU keeps two-handedness: `if (group < Bows && width == 2)` sets IsTwoHandedWeaponEquipped. One here, and MuWeapons.cs says TwoHanded: false, so the two agree and the shield hand stays free.
stats.height_note: Height is the sixth argument of the call above and was not carried across when this row was first transcribed - see width_note, which explains why width was. Both are needed now that the bag has a footprint: an item occupies a rectangle of the inventory grid rather than one cell, so a Small Axe is one across and three down, and drawing it in a single square is what made every weapon read as a thumbnail. See Satchel.Covered, which walks the rectangle.
stats.attack_speed_note: Twenty against the Kris's fifty, and it is the Kris that is the outlier rather than this: 20 is what the Small Axe carries and what most of the low table carries. So the first sword swings at the pace of the first axe, and the Kris - which a Budge Dragon cannot leave - is the fast one you have to go up a level to find.
stats.classes_from: The last three ints of the call are 1, 1, 1 - wizard, knight, elf - which MuWeapons.cs states as the same flag set from the client's side. Sixty strength with no level requirement is the one gate on it.

stance_from: MuWeapons.cs: WeaponStance.Sword, one-handed. Actions 4 and 17, the same family the Kris and the Small Axe use.
sheet_from: Data/NPC/sword03.OZJ (256x64), from MuMain. Sword02.bmd names sword03.jpg, which is Data/Item/sword03.OZJ at 128x32.
sheet_note:
The Sword01 case again, and it had to be checked rather than assumed. find_source turns up three copies of sword03: MuMain's Item at 128x32, MuMain's NPC at 256x64, and remaster_one's Item at 256x64. Both larger ones are exactly 2x the small one, which is the upscale signature the tool warns about by name, so the size on its own decides nothing.

Looked at side by side, magnified, the NPC copy carries drawn detail the Item copy has no trace of: a row of dark engraved accent marks along the inner curve of the guard, hatching across the lower quillon, and grain in the black leather of the grip. In the Item copy those three areas are flat gradients. An enlargement smooths what is there and hardens boundaries; it does not put localised dark marks into the middle of a gradient. So the NPC copy is MU's art at the size MU drew it, exactly as Data/NPC/sword02 was for the Kris.

remaster_one's 256x64 is a third distinct file at the same size, which is what settles the other half of it: two different 2x versions of one 128x32 drawing cannot both be MU's, and the one in the tree whose Data/Player was upscaled in place is the one that is not.
material_note:
Three islands, three materials, and the sheet separates them cleanly enough that this is measured rather than judged. Sampled per triangle at its own UV centre rather than by island bounding box - the reading the polearms taught, and necessary here because island 1's box overlaps the blade's and a box mean would have called the guard steel.

The chroma is what decides it. Island 2's twelve triangles are the blade and are achromatic: max-minus-min channel of 6 to 19 across means around (190-233, 200-249, 201-246), which is pale blue-white and nothing else. Island 1's twenty are the guard and are not: chroma 90 to 118 about means of (230, 216, 140), (223, 194, 127) and (224, 186, 106), which is gold. Island 0's are dark and flat - (55, 48, 57) at chroma 10 - which is unlit black leather.

So steel on the blade, brass on the guard, leather_wrap on the grip. brass rather than a second gold: its own file argues for exactly this case - "MU painted the guard a different colour and nothing else; a modern material can say it is a different surface" - and 0.44 rough against the blade's 0.32 is the difference that says cast fitting rather than ground edge.
open_question:
Island 0 is the grip and the pommel cap together, and they are not the same thing. Eight of its twelve triangles are the dark achromatic leather at u 0.888 to 0.944; the other four are at the sheet's far right edge, u 0.999, and sample (170, 123, 80) at chroma 89 - a brown-gold end cap, which is a fitting and belongs with the guard.

The island is the unit, as it was on the Battle Axe, the Dragon Lance and the Great Scythe, so it takes the majority reading and the cap ships as leather-roughness metal-coloured albedo. Four triangles at the butt of the grip is the cheapest instance of this limit in the project so far, and splitting it would need assignment finer than an island.
material_overrides_note: Steel at 0.4 here rather than the library's 0.2. A broad flat blade held side-on mirrors whatever is beside it, which in the hand is the grass, and at 0.2 it rendered near black (2026-09-21). Rougher, the reflection blurs to a grey sheen with a soft highlight. The thin and curved blades keep 0.2 because they turn some face to the sky.
